titre: 1968: A Demo Already Shows the Mouse, Hypertext, Video Calls
accroche: On December 9, 1968, Douglas Engelbart presents the mouse, hypertext, and screen sharing in 90 minutes, twenty years before their spread.
contenu_vulgarise:
On December 9, 1968, about a thousand engineers and computer scientists gather at San Francisco's Civic Auditorium for the Fall Joint Computer Conference. On a giant screen, borrowed from NASA Ames, appears Douglas Engelbart, seated at a workstation connected by phone line to an SDS 940 computer at the Augmentation Research Center of the Stanford Research Institute (SRI), nearly thirty kilometers away, in Menlo Park.

## One demonstration, four inventions

For ninety minutes, Engelbart runs live through a system he calls NLS, for oN-Line System. He types text, corrects it, cuts it and pastes it elsewhere in the document. He clicks on words to open other documents linked to them, what will later be called hypertext. He opens several windows on screen at once. He switches to his colleague Bill Paxton, still in Menlo Park, who edits the same document live, on the same screen, while they talk over video link.

To point and click, Engelbart uses a wooden case with two wheels, fitted with a cord that hangs from the back like a tail: that is why his team nicknamed it the “mouse.” He had filed the patent for it back in 1967, under the name “X-Y position indicator for a display system,” with engineer Bill English, who built it. In the room, the reception is enthusiastic.

## Twenty years ahead, with almost nothing to show for it

None of this was then on the market: neither the mouse, nor word processing, nor cut-and-paste, nor video conferencing would become mass-market products before the late 1980s, when Apple and Microsoft took them up. Meanwhile, Engelbart's laboratory, the Augmentation Research Center, loses most of its funding during the 1970s, and several of its engineers leave to work at Xerox PARC, where their ideas find more fertile ground and feed into the interface that will, in turn, inspire the Macintosh.

Engelbart himself will never receive a royalty on the mouse patent. His public recognition has to wait for the 1990s: the Lemelson-MIT Prize, worth $500,000, in 1997, then the National Medal of Technology, awarded by President Clinton in 2000. He dies in 2013, at eighty-eight, holding twenty patents. Being right twenty years ahead of everyone else, this story shows, is not enough to reap the rewards: the rest of the world also has to be ready to seize them.

repere.texte: On December 9, 1968, at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco, Douglas Engelbart presents the mouse, hypertext, word processing, and live video conferencing in a single ninety-minute demonstration, before about a thousand computing professionals.
repere.source: SRI International, Doug Engelbart Video Archives (Internet Archive); Lemelson-MIT Program

carte.punch: In 1968, one man showed off the personal computer, twenty years too soon
carte.idee: On December 9, 1968, Douglas Engelbart presents the mouse, hypertext, word processing, and video conferencing in a single 90-minute demonstration. His lab will lose its funding within the decade, and he will never receive a royalty on the mouse patent.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The original recording, held by SRI International on Internet Archive.

quiz.question: Why didn't Engelbart's 1968 demonstration immediately change computing?
choix: Because the audience, made up of engineers, did not see the link to their own research
Because his laboratory lost its funding in the 1970s, despite the enthusiastic reception
Because the demonstration was cut short before the end, due to an unstable connection
Because no patent had been filed on the technologies shown
quiz.explication: The audience applauded the demonstration, but that was not enough: the Augmentation Research Center lost its funding in the 1970s, and several key engineers left for Xerox PARC, where these ideas found a second wind before reaching the public in the 1980s.
